name: International Refugee Assistance Project: litigation and policy (charityevals' estimate)
beneficiaries_note: Our build: by share of the result at the defaults: the SIV plan (about 27%: Afghans 90%, Iraqis 10%), the US refugee programme's rebuild (about 70%, spread over the largest nationalities of fiscal year 2024 admissions: the DR Congo, Afghanistan, Venezuela, Syria, Burma, Guatemala, a judgment) and the Pacito refugees (3%, Congolese like the lead plaintiff).
summary: IRAP's litigation, policy and communications work ($6.3 million in the year to August 2025, $5.4 million a year on average over fiscal years 2021-2025 in 2025 prices) is counted as a past average over the wins of those five years: IRAP's defence and revision of the court-ordered plan that speeds Special Immigrant Visas for Afghan and Iraqi allies (about 27,000 visas a year, judged a quarter of a year sooner), a share of the rebuilt US refugee programme (100,034 admissions in fiscal year 2024 against 11,411 in 2021, until the suspension of January 2025) and the 80 refugees resettled under its 2025 injunctions in Pacito v. Trump, each valued as in charityevals' model of IRAP's legal services by the move's consumption gain and deaths averted. With advocacy judged to have caused 8% of the rebuild and IRAP's share of the coalition at 6%, and its next dollar at {{row:marginal_vs_past_average}} of the average, it comes to about {{result}} years of healthy life per 1,000 dollars, because a won pathway moves thousands of people for the cost of one campaign. The result is mostly uncertainty, its own ranges alone spanning over a thousandfold (advocacy's share of the rebuild and IRAP's share of the coalition, how much sooner the visas came); all three branches are discounted by the shared missing-data slider.

source.page: Table 3, Iraqi and Afghan SIV recipients by fiscal year (principals, dependents, total): 2022 11,954; 2023 27,318; 2024 22,942 through 31 March 2024

rows.explainer: The people the court-ordered processing plan in Afghan and Iraqi Allies v. Blinken covers each year: principals and their families issued visas in a full year under the plan (fiscal year 2024 ran at a similar pace: 22,942 by 31 March 2024, the same table). IRAP brought the class action in 2018; the court ordered the government to process applications promptly under a plan with deadlines for its own steps, and in the period IRAP defended the plan against the government's motion to end it (district court, late 2022; D.C. Circuit, June 2024). Range: 20,000 (between fiscal year 2022's 11,954, the ramp-up after the withdrawal, and 2023's figure) to about 45,000 (fiscal year 2024's first half, 22,942, at a full year's pace).

rows.label: Years sooner each visa holder reaches safety because of the plan
rows.explainer: The reference class for the delays is the State Department Inspector General's 2020 review of the Afghan programme: staffing stayed flat while the backlog grew, and some applicants spent more than three years in administrative processing against the nine months the law sets. No study measures how much a court-ordered timetable shortens such a line; with visas, staff and vetting still the limits, a deadline speeds the line rather than lengthening it, by little: our judgment a quarter of a year sooner on average, from a few weeks to nine months.

rows.label: Consumption per person a day of visa applicants waiting in Afghanistan or Iraq (2021 PPP dollars)
rows.explainer: Most waiting applicants are Afghans in Afghanistan under the Taliban, where incomes collapsed after 2021, or in Pakistan; Iraqis are better off. Anchored on Kenya's survey mean of 4.44 a day (@survey_consumption.ken_survey_mean_2021ppp_day), above Afghanistan's; our judgment 2.5, from 1.5 to 5.

rows.label: Share of the deaths averted that are of children under five

rows.label: Share of the period's faster processing owed to the period's own defence and revision of the plan
rows.explainer: The court ordered the processing plan on 14 June 2020 (before the cost period, fiscal years 2021-2025); the suit ran from 2018. In the period IRAP defended the plan against the government's attempts to end it and had it revised after the 2021 withdrawal, when it was 'paused for revisions' (CRS R43725): district court late 2022, D.C. Circuit June 2024 (IRAP's case page and the court's opinion). Only that defence and revision is credited here, and processing also sped up because of the withdrawal, Congress's new visa numbers and political pressure: our judgment 20%, from 8% to 50%.

rows.explainer: The shared IRAP figure (facts/irap.json).

rows.label: Share of the rebuild that advocacy caused
rows.explainer: The Biden administration raised the ceiling and funded the rebuild as its own policy, but advocacy demonstrably moved it: in April 2021 the administration kept the previous administration's 15,000 ceiling, and after an outcry from advocates and members of Congress it raised it to 62,500 in May 2021 (Presidential Determination on Refugee Admissions, 3 May 2021). Advocates (the Refugee Advocacy Lab IRAP co-founded, Refugee Council USA, resettlement agencies, state and local officials' letters) then pressed for faster rebuilding and new channels (NGO referrals, private sponsorship). Anchored on that episode, where advocacy changed one decision but not the administration's direction, our judgment is that advocacy caused 8% of the extra admissions, from 2% to 20%.

rows.formula: usrap_extra_per_year * lifetime_value_per_person * usrap_p_success * pv_annuity_due(1, $discount_rate, usrap_years_counted) / campaign_years

rows.explainer: 1: what would have come without the litigation is the share in siv_p_success (Convention 5, one question each).

rows.label: IRAP's share of the resources behind the SIV case
rows.explainer: IRAP is lead counsel with pro bono co-counsel (Freshfields Bruckhaus Deringer) giving many hours; our judgment 0.5, from 0.3 to 0.8.

rows.label: This charity's share of the good done with money, work or budgets it brings in
rows.explainer: The site's one setting for resources another party commits only because of the organisation (docs/normalization.md 2.24): governments' budgets and enforcement, companies' compliance, the use others make of research. The charity is credited this share of the good done with them, net of their cost; the rest stays with those who paid or did the work. Fixed.

rows.label: Share of credit used: IRAP's share of the resources behind the SIV case
rows.explainer: The share among those who paid for or did the same work, times the mobiliser's share: the rest of the credit stays with those who carry out or adopt the result (docs/normalization.md 2.24).

rows.label: Share of the extra refugees admitted who wouldn't have reached safety another way
rows.explainer: A different question from advocacy's share of the rebuild: would these refugees have got to safety anyway (another resettlement country, family reunification, onward migration)? UNHCR's yearly Projected Global Resettlement Needs reports put the refugees in need of resettlement at well over a million a year, against global resettlement departures of around 100,000 to 200,000, so few would have; 0.85, from 0.7 to 1.

rows.label: IRAP's share of the advocacy coalition's resources
rows.explainer: Dozens of groups pressed for the rebuild, the resettlement agencies largest among them; IRAP co-founded the Refugee Advocacy Lab and led its letters of elected officials (380 in 2022, over 300 in 2025). Our judgment 6%, from 2% to 15%.

rows.label: Share of credit used: IRAP's share of the advocacy coalition's resources
rows.explainer: The share among those who paid for or did the same work, times the mobiliser's share: the rest of the credit stays with those who carry out or adopt the result (docs/normalization.md 2.24).

rows.label: Share of the Pacito arrivals that wouldn't have come anyway
rows.explainer: Without the injunctions, a few of these refugees might have travelled under the ban's case-by-case exceptions or after a later lifting; 0.7, from 0.4 to 0.9.

rows.label: IRAP's share of the resources behind Pacito v. Trump
rows.explainer: IRAP leads the case with pro bono co-counsel and plaintiff organisations (resettlement agencies); 0.5, from 0.3 to 0.8.

rows.label: Share of credit used: IRAP's share of the resources behind Pacito v. Trump
rows.explainer: The share among those who paid for or did the same work, times the mobiliser's share: the rest of the credit stays with those who carry out or adopt the result (docs/normalization.md 2.24).

rows.label: Other wins of the period, as a share of the three modelled
rows.explainer: Wins not modelled one by one: family reunification parole for Central Americans and Colombians (2023, which IRAP 'helped design and advance', ended 2025), the Central American Minors programme's enhancements (2023), the NGO referral channel to US resettlement, European family-reunification rulings (a German passport precedent), state laws, and the court order restoring services to recently arrived refugees (Pacito, 2025); the climate-displacement work has no win yet. A share of the three modelled branches: 0.3, from 0 to 1.

rows.label: Backlash and losses, as a share of modelled value
rows.explainer: High-profile litigation against the administration can harden policy; little evidence either way; -2%, from -10% to 0.

rows.label: Safety and family reunion beyond consumption, as a share
rows.explainer: As in the legal-services model: consumption misses the relief of safety and reunited families; 10%, from 0 to 30%.

rows.label: Remittances to family left behind, less early costs to host countries, as a share
rows.explainer: As in the legal-services model: resettled refugees send money to relatives still waiting; host countries pay reception costs in the first years, mostly repaid in taxes later. Net slightly positive, from -5% to +10%.

rows.label: Benefits and harms not modelled, as a share of modelled value
rows.explainer: The sum of the three shares above.
